texts.label: text
texts.orig: Morbidity following cardiac surgery has increased in high-risk patients undergoing complex procedures [1]. Many studies [2,3] have demonstrated that perioperative goal-directed therapy (GDT) aimed at hemodynamic goals can decrease postoperative morbidity during major surgery. However, using GDT to increase oxygen delivery, in an effort to reduce oxygen debt (a cumulative deficit of oxygen available for oxidative metabolism) and morbidity following cardiac surgery, is controversial [4,5].

texts.orig: Increasing the depth of anesthesia target goals to decrease oxygen consumption is also effective in optimizing the cerebral oxygen balance [14]. Unfortunately, deep anesthesia, demonstrated by a low bispectral index score (BIS; cumulative time with a BIS < 45), has been independently associated with postoperative mortality following cardiac surgery [15]. Our observational study showed that the BIS should be maintained at > 45 in high-risk patients [16]. However, 50%-75% of high-risk patients experienced one or more episodes of rScO2 desaturation during CPB [17]. Thus, to optimize cerebral oxygen balance, a BIS of 40-45 during CPB may be better [18].

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Previous studies [8,9] have shown the benefits of preventing decreases in rScO2 levels during cardiac surgery in general patients, but not in high-risk populations (who underwent combined surgery, or multiple valve replacement and/or redo surgery). For example, a multicenter prospective study [17] failed to show that reversing decreases in rScO2 levels could benefit high-risk patients undergoing CPB. A systematic review [19] did not support the hypothesis that goal-directed optimization of rScO2 has clinical benefits in cardiac surgery. However, no data have shown an association between a comprehensive strategy(an individualized GDT based on cerebral oxygen balance) and postoperative morbidity and mortality. Here, individualized GDT defined as individualized targets of a less than 20% decline in the rScO2/ MAP level from baseline and a BIS of 45-60 during non-CPB as well as a BIS of 40-45 during CPB. To address this issue, we conducted a randomized, controlled, prospective study designed to investigate whether the implementation of a new individualized therapy protocol in highrisk patients undergoing cardiac surgery could yield better outcomes than standard care.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Patients who were 18 years old or older and scheduled for cardiac surgery were screened for enrollment. Patients undergoing valvular surgery and/or coronary artery bypass grafting with CPB who met one of the following high-risk criteria were included: A European System for Cardiac Operative Risk Evaluation score ≥ 6, a left ventricular ejection fraction < 50%, or a combined cardiac surgical procedure. Patients were excluded from the trial if one of the following was present: Emergency surgery; ventricular assist device implantation; stage five chronic kidney disease; a history of anesthesia awareness; or refusal of consent.

texts.orig: 2.4. Standard treatment
texts.text: 2.4. Standard treatment

texts.label: text
texts.orig: For all patients, bilateral near-infrared spectroscopy sensors (INVOS TM 5100C; Covidien, USA) were used to measure the rScO2 levels and the BIS values were measured with a BIS monitor (VISTA, Covidien, USA). For patients in the usual care group, intraoperative hemodynamic management was performed according to institutional protocols based on standard measures to achieve the following: A heart rate in the range of 60-100 beats/min; central venous oxygen saturation (ScVO2) > 70%; lactate levels < 3 mmol/L; hematocrit values > 28%; and urinary output > 0.5 mL/kg/h. Interventions included a fluid resuscitation with lactated Ringer's solution, administration of norepinephrine or dobutamine (if the cardiac index remained below 3.0 L/ min/m 2 ), and a red blood cell (RBC) transfusion. A target MAP of 65 mmHg was maintained.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In the individualized GDT group, interventions were performed by the anesthesiologist in the operating room. The intraoperative intervention was aimed to meet the following goals: A less than 20% decline in the rScO2 level from baseline; a less than 20% decline in the MAP from baseline; a BIS of 45-60 before and after CPB; and a BIS of 40-45 during CPB.

The intraoperative intervention was aimed to meet the following goals: A less than 20% decline in the rScO2 level from baseline; a less than 20% decline in the MAP from baseline; a BIS of 45-60 before and after CPB; and a BIS of 40-45 during CPB.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: rScO2 intervention commenced following an algorithm (Supplement S2) as proposed by Murkin et al. [14] if the rScO2 value decreased below 80% from baseline for 1 min or longer. During CPB, it included the pump flow was increased to 2.5 L/min/m 2 if a cardiac index was < 2.0 L/min/m 2 ; checking head position and venous cannula position to ensure adequate venous drainage; maintaining jugular venous pressure < 10 mmHg by repositioning the heart during bypass; the increasing fraction of inspiration O2 to 1.0; increasing depth of anesthesia to decrease cerebral oxygen consumption; optimizing PaCO2 (maintain PaCO2 close to 5.3 kPa). A similar intervention was performed to adjust MAP to a less than 20% decline from baseline values. Initially, a continuous infusion of 2-4 mL/kg/h lactated Ringer solution was used. After a maximum of 0.1 μg/kg/min norepinephrine intravenous infusion, fluid resuscitation was provided by administration of 150-200 mL of lactated Ringer solution boluses if the stroke volume index was less than 35 mL/m 2 . If the cardiac index remained below 3.0 L/min/m 2 , dobutamine infusion was started at 5 μg/kg/min. If these interventions did not result in a cardiac index greater than 3.0 L/ min/m 2 , red blood cells (RBCs) were transfused 1 unit at a time to achieve a hematocrit value higher than 28%. To optimize cerebral oxygen balance, propofol concentrations were adjusted to maintain a BIS in the range of 45-60 before and after CPB and of 40-45 during CPB.

texts.orig: 2.6. Anesthesia and CPB management
texts.text: 2.6. Anesthesia and CPB management

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Baseline hemodynamic data were obtained 10 min after a small amount of midazolam (0.02 mg/kg) was administered. Baseline rScO2 values were obtained after the patients had been resting quietly for at least 1 min while receiving 3-5 L/min of O2 by nasal cannula with a stabilized signal. General anesthesia was usually induced with 1 μg/kg of sufentanil, a smooth target-controlled infusion of propofol (with an initial target concentration of 1.0 μg/mL), and 0.6 mg/kg rocuronium. Before the intervention period, a specialist in echocardiography measured the cardiac index with the use of a transesophageal echocardiogram. A cardiac output monitor (LiDCOrapid, London, United Kingdom) was connected to the arterial cable, and The LiDCOrapid was calibrated at baseline by inputting the cardiac index value obtained by the echocardiogram. During CPB, pump flow was kept at a rate of 2.0-2.5 L/min/m 2 , with rectal temperature in the range of 32 °C-35 °C during α-stat pH management, and a PaO2 in the range of 150-200 mmHg. After surgery, all patients were transferred still intubated to the intensive care unit (ICU).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: To achieve significance, we calculated that a sample of 128 patients would be required for a reduction in the composite endpoint incidence from 50% in the usual care group [21] to 25% in the GDT group (accounting for a two-sided α-level of 0.05, a statistical power of 80%, and allowing for a loss to follow-up of 10%).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: A modified intention-to-treat analysis was conducted, including all randomized participants who had at least one post-baseline measurement of the primary outcome, with exclusions for missing data and deviations from the protocol. Continuous variables were reported as medians with interquartile ranges (IQRs). Categorical variables were reported as proportions. Continuous variables were compared with a Student t -test (parametric) or Mann-Whitney U test (non-parametric), and categorical variables were subjected to Pearson chi-square analysis, Fisher's exact test, or likelihood ratio tests. Primary and secondary outcomes are reported as relative risk (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Kaplan-Meier curves were constructed to analyze eventfree survival probabilities for 30 days following surgery. To determine the predictors of postoperative major complications, a post-hoc logistic regression model using a backward stepwise methodology was used. The threshold for inclusion in the model was selected at P < 0.05. The Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test was used to assess the fit of the model, while the performance of the model was assessed using the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve and the associated c-statistic.

texts.orig: A greater portion of patients achieved their preoperative individual targets in the individualized GDT group (47/65 [72%]) as compared to the control group (28/63 [44%]). Our secondary analysis showed that the achievement of a patient's predefined target, adjusted for a group, was associated with a reduction in major morbidity risk in the 30-day postoperative period (RR 3.41, 95% CI 2.19-5.31, P < 0.001; Table 4). Furthermore, the achievement of oxygen balance targets was associated with reduced incidences of infection, low cardiac output syndrome, stroke, and delirium morbidity in the 30-day postoperative period. Moreover, the achievement of oxygen balance targets reduced the length of the ICU ( P =0.001) and hospital stays ( P < 0.001), with no difference in mortality (1% vs. 9%, respectively; P = 0.16). Cardiac surgery patients with a significant decrease in rScO2 levels from baseline are at an increased risk of major organ dysfunction [14]. This finding has led to clinicians seeking strategies to reverse the decrease in rScO2 levels during cardiac surgery, with the aim of enhancing cerebral oxygenation and global tissue perfusion to reduce the incidence of postoperative complications [23]. For example, absolute cerebral desaturation is an important predictor of postoperative delirium [24]. The main effective therapeutic measures to restore cerebral desaturation include increasing the MAP and adjusting the depth of anesthesia [9]. However, a previous study [25] showed that a low MAP and BIS during cardiac surgery were each independently associated with poorer outcomes. Therefore, we selected a comprehensive strategy of simultaneously optimizing the MAP, BIS, and rScO2 levels for our patient cohort.

texts.orig: The strengths of this study include its innovative trial design, which focused on comprehensive strategies. Prior trials [32,33] have not used systematically individualized GDT based on oxygen balance targets, and rather employed the population-based values associated with improved clinical outcomes from observational studies. Furthermore, in the current study, a secondary analysis was used to compare the outcomes between the target achievers and non-achievers. We have demonstrated that the achievement of individual targets based on cerebral oxygen balance is potentially associated with reduced postoperative morbidity. These data suggest that an enhanced mechanistic understanding of the consequences of oxygen balance management could reveal novel strategies to improve surgical critical care outcomes.

texts.orig: This study does have several limitations. Firstly, as an a priori assumption, we hypothesized a 50% reduction in the incidence of overall complications, according to a similar reduction suggested from several previous studies [9,14,21]. However, it was hard to expect an effect of this magnitude. Indeed, if we had instead aimed for a reduction in the composite endpoint (i.e., of 10% or 15%), the sample size would have been increased and it would have been highly likely that some of the primary outcomes, such as infection or stroke, would have then become significant based on the existence of very strong trends towards significance within the lower sample size. This is an important limitation and warrants further investigation. Secondly, in secondary analysis, we added some patients from the control group to the interventional group and significant differences were found between the newly developed groups. Although this was interesting, the power of the trial is a matter of concern. However, assuming a significance level of 5% and a power of 80%, 46 patients per group would be needed to detect a clinically important 50% absolute reduction in morbidity (the morbidity in the non-achiever group was more than 70%). This factor did not reduce the power of the trial. Moreover, the crossover of intraoperative predefined targets achievers in the control group was substantially higher than we had anticipated. This factor alone reduced the power of the trial but did not alter several key observations. A large-scale randomized controlled trial would be needed to confirm the benefit of individualized targets based on oxygen balance in this population of patients.
